en_version: Midrash Tanhuma-Yelammedenu, trans. Samuel A. Berman
he: ‎בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים, זֶה שֶׁאָמַר הַכָּתוּב: בְּרָכוֹת לְרֹאשׁ צַדִּיק וּפִי רְשָׁעִים יְכַסֶּה חָמָס (משלי י, ה). לָמָּה פָתַח בִּבְרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם בְּבֵי״‎ת וְלֹא בְאָלֶ״‎ף, וַהֲלֹא אָלֶ״‎ף רֹאשׁ לְכָל הָאוֹתִיּוֹת? אֶלָּא לְפִי שֶׁהָאָלֶ״‎ף לָשׁוֹן אָרוּר וּבֵי״‎ת לָשׁוֹן בָּרוּךְ, אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, אֶבְרָא אֶת הָעוֹלָם בִּלְשׁוֹן בָּרוּךְ. וּמָה, כְשֶׁנִּבְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן בָּרוּךְ, בְּנֵי אָדָם מַכְעִיסִין לְיוֹצְרָם. בִּלְשׁוֹן אָרוּר עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
en: In the beginning God created (Gen. 1:1). It is written elsewhere in reference to this verse: Blessings are upon the head of the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked concealeth violence (Prov. 10:6). Why did the Holy One, blessed be He, commence the account of the creation of His world with the letter bet rather than with the alef, the first letter of the alphabet? He did so because the alef is the first letter of the word arur (“cursed”), while the bet is the first letter of the word barukh (“blessed”). The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “I will begin the account of the creation of the world with the letter that symbolizes a blessing.” Even though the account of the creation of the world starts with a letter that symbolizes a blessing, mankind angered its Creator. How much angrier would man have made Him if the creation narrative had commenced with the letter that symbolizes a curse!
